title: Glossary
markdown:
Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Address** | The number of a byte in memory. (4.03) |
| **ALU** | Arithmetic logic unit: the part of the CPU that adds, subtracts and does logic on bits. (4.02) |
| **ARM64** | The instruction set of phones, tablets and Apple-chip Macs. (1.05) |
| **ASCII** | The 1963 table giving English characters the numbers 0 to 127. (3.01) |
| **Assembler** | A program that translates assembly language into machine code. (5.01) |
| **Assembly language** | Machine instructions written as names (`mov`, `add`) and labels; one line per instruction. (5.01) |
| **Binary** | Base 2: counting with only 0 and 1, each place worth twice the one to its right. (2.02) |
| **Bit** | One binary digit: 0 or 1. (1.01) |
| **Boot loader** | The small program that loads the operating system's kernel. (6.05) |
| **Byte** | 8 bits; the unit memory is counted in. (2.03) |
| **Bytecode** | Instructions for a virtual machine rather than a real CPU (Java, C#, Python). (5.03) |
| **Cache** | A small, fast memory holding copies of recently used data. (4.06) |
| **Carry** | The 1 passed to the next column when a column's sum is too big. (2.05) |
| **Code point** | The number Unicode gives a character, written U+ and hex. (3.01) |
| **Compiler** | A program that translates a high-level language into machine code before it runs. (5.02) |
| **Context switch** | Saving one thread's registers and loading another's. (6.02) |
| **Core** | One complete processor; a chip has several. (1.05) |
| **CPU** | Central processing unit: fetches and executes instructions. (1.01) |
| **DNS** | The system that turns names like example.com into IP addresses. (6.06) |
| **Driver** | Kernel code that controls one kind of device. (6.04) |
| **Encoding** | An agreed table turning characters into numbers (ASCII, UTF-8). (3.01) |
| **Endianness** | Which byte of a multi-byte number comes first in memory: little-endian (lowest first) or big-endian. (2.06) |
| **Executable** | A file of machine code the operating system can run. (3.05) |
| **Fetch, decode, execute** | The cycle every CPU repeats. (4.04) |
| **File descriptor** | The number a process uses for an open file: 0 input, 1 output, 2 errors. (6.04) |
| **File system** | The kernel's organisation of disk blocks into named files and folders. (6.04) |
| **Firmware** | Software stored in a chip on the motherboard (UEFI, BIOS) that starts the computer. (6.05) |
| **Flip-flop** | A circuit of gates that stores one bit. (4.03) |
| **Floating point** | Storing numbers like scientific notation in binary; approximate for most fractions. (3.03) |
| **Font** | A set of glyphs, one shape per character. (3.02) |
| **Framebuffer** | The memory holding the colour of every pixel on screen. (3.02) |
| **GPU** | A chip with thousands of simple cores, for graphics and AI. (1.05) |
| **Hexadecimal** | Base 16, digits 0 to 9 and A to F; one digit is four bits. (2.04) |
| **High-level language** | A language that lets you write what you mean, translated to machine code by a compiler or interpreter. (5.02) |
| **Instruction set** | The instructions a CPU family understands, and their encoding (x86-64, ARM64). (1.05) |
| **Integrated circuit** | Many transistors and their connections made on one chip of silicon. (1.04) |
| **Interpreter** | A program that carries out another program as it reads it. (5.03) |
| **Interrupt** | A hardware signal that makes the CPU jump into the kernel. (6.02) |
| **IP address** | The number that says where a packet goes: 32 bits (IPv4) or 128 bits (IPv6). (6.06) |
| **JIT** | Just-in-time compilation: compiling the busy parts of a program while it runs. (5.03) |
| **Kernel** | The core of the operating system; the only code allowed to touch hardware. (6.01) |
| **Kernel mode** | The CPU's privileged mode, for the kernel. (6.01) |
| **Linker** | Joins compiled pieces and libraries into one executable. (5.03) |
| **Logic gate** | A circuit giving one bit out from bits in: NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND. (4.01) |
| **Machine code** | A program as the bytes a CPU executes. (4.05) |
| **Magic number** | Fixed bytes at the start of a file saying what format it is. (3.05) |
| **Microprocessor** | A whole CPU on one chip. (1.04) |
| **Moore's law** | The observation that transistors per chip doubled about every two years. (1.04) |
| **Nibble** | 4 bits: one hexadecimal digit. (2.03) |
| **Operating system** | The software that runs the computer for every other program. (6.01) |
| **Overflow** | A result too big for the bits it is stored in, which then wraps around. (2.05) |
| **Packet** | A small piece of data sent across a network with its own address. (6.06) |
| **Page** | A block of memory (usually 4 KiB) mapped as a unit by virtual memory. (6.03) |
| **Pixel** | One dot of a picture or screen, stored as a colour. (3.04) |
| **Pointer** | A value that holds an address. (4.03) |
| **Process** | A program while it runs, with its own memory. (6.02) |
| **Program counter** | The register holding the address of the next instruction. (4.04) |
| **RAM** | Main memory: fast, and forgets everything without power. (4.03) |
| **Register** | A tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. (4.03) |
| **RGB** | Red, green and blue light: three numbers that make a colour. (3.04) |
| **Scheduler** | The kernel part that shares CPU cores between threads. (6.02) |
| **Segmentation fault** | A crash from touching memory the process does not own. (6.03) |
| **Stored program** | Keeping the program in the same memory as its data. (1.03) |
| **System call** | A request from a program to the kernel, made with a special instruction. (5.06) |
| **TCP** | The protocol that makes delivery over the internet reliable and in order. (6.06) |
| **Thread** | One line of execution inside a process. (6.02) |
| **Transistor** | An electronic switch made of silicon; billions make a chip. (1.04) |
| **Truth table** | Every input of a logic circuit and its output. (4.01) |
| **Turing machine** | Turing's simple imaginary computer, able to compute anything computable. (1.03) |
| **Two's complement** | The way computers store negative numbers: flip the bits and add one. (2.05) |
| **Unicode** | One table giving every character of every language its own number. (3.01) |
| **User mode** | The CPU's restricted mode, for apps. (6.01) |
| **UTF-8** | The usual way to store Unicode as bytes: 1 to 4 per character, ASCII unchanged. (3.01) |
| **Virtual machine** | A program that runs bytecode for an imaginary computer (the JVM). (5.03) |
| **Virtual memory** | Each process's private addresses, translated to real RAM by the CPU. (6.03) |
| **x86-64** | The instruction set of most PCs and servers. (1.05) |
